It is not recommended to implement certain interventions in primary health-care facilities due to the conditional strength of recommendation and the low quality of evidence supporting them. 2. At primary health-care facilities, health workers should provide nutritional counseling to caregivers of overweight children under the age of 5. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low-quality evidence. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) child growth standards include methods for assessing length/height-for-age, weight-for-age, weight-for-length, weight-for-height, and body mass index-for-age. 4. Updates on the management of severe acute malnutrition in infants and children are available in specific WHO guidelines. 5. Indicators for assessing food insecurity are outlined in the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) Global Partners publication. 6. At primary health-care facilities, health workers should counsel caregivers of overweight children under 5 years of age on physical activity. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low-quality evidence. 7. Children under 5 years of age identified as obese should be assessed, and an appropriate management plan should be developed. This can be done by adequately trained health workers at the primary health-care level or at referral clinics or local hospitals. The strength of this recommendation is conditional, with moderate-quality evidence. 8. The global epidemic of childhood and adolescent obesity affects all regions, including countries where undernutrition remains prevalent. In 2016, an estimated 41 million children under 5 years of age (6.0%) were affected by overweight or obesity, representing an increase of about 11 million since 2000. 9. In 2016, nearly half (49%) of overweight children under 5 lived in Asia, and 24% lived in Africa. 10. The 2012 Global Burden of Disease study reported for the first time that more people died from overnutrition than undernutrition. 11. Demographic and nutritional transitions are occurring in low-income countries, even where undernutrition is common. Overweight and obesity in children and adolescents have immediate physical and mental health implications and are major risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and premature death in adulthood. 12. The prevalence of childhood obesity reflects shifts toward unhealthy diets and reduced physical activity. Factors such as urbanization, market liberalization, increased incomes, fast food availability, educational demands, motorized transport, television viewing, and gaming have contributed to increased consumption of high-fat, high-sugar, and high-salt foods, along with lower levels of physical activity. 13. Individual-level drivers of childhood obesity include maternal nutrition during pregnancy, infant and child feeding practices, population dietary patterns, and lifestyle factors such as decreased physical activity and increased sedentary behavior. 14. Children born with low birth weight, who have experienced undernutrition, or who have stunted growth are at greater risk of developing overweight and obesity when exposed to energy-dense diets and sedentary lifestyles later in life. 15. The WHO Global Strategy for Infant and Young Child Feeding outlines essential interventions to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding and complementary feeding. In settings where undernutrition is common, the use of commercial breast-milk substitutes is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. 16. The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) is an approach to child health that focuses on the well-being of the whole child. It aims to reduce death, illness, and disability while promoting growth and development among children under 5 years of age. 17. IMCI includes preventive and therapeutic elements implemented by families, communities, and health workers. It promotes accurate identification of childhood illnesses, appropriate combined treatment, caregiver counseling, and timely referral of severely ill children. 18. IMCI does not currently provide guidance on the assessment and management of overweight or obese children, despite the global epidemic of childhood obesity. 19. WHO guidelines should be reviewed to ensure that recommendations for addressing moderate acute malnutrition do not inadvertently increase the risk of obesity and noncommunicable diseases later in life. 20. This guideline aims to provide guidance on the assessment and management of infants and children at primary health-care facilities to reduce the risk of overweight and obesity, particularly in settings where undernutrition and obesity coexist. 21. The guideline is intended for use in lowand medium-resource settings and targets national policymakers, development partners, program managers, health-care providers, researchers, and clinicians managing infants and children. 22. Successful implementation of the guideline will require appropriate training and capacity development of health-care workers, as well as systematic monitoring and evaluation of programs to identify and address challenges. 23. The guideline will contribute to efforts by Member States and their partners to make informed decisions on appropriate nutrition actions to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and global nutrition targets.
